hook.question: Your phone holds 10,000 songs. Tap song number 7,342 and it starts at once. How does it find that song without counting past the first 7,341?
paragraphs: If you were walking along a shelf of 10,000 records, you would count your way there, and a longer shelf would mean a longer walk. Yet the phone takes the same tiny moment for song 7,342 as for song 1.
Here is the clue. The songs sit in one unbroken row of boxes, all the same size, and the phone knows where the first box starts.
hook.aha: Same-size boxes in an unbroken row turn counting into arithmetic: the box you want is at start + number × box size. One multiply and one add, whether the box is number 7 or number 7,000. That is an array. The price is that the row must stay unbroken, so squeezing a new box into the middle means moving everything after it.

metaphor: Picture a corridor of lockers, all the same width, bolted side by side and numbered from 0 at the door.
To reach locker 7 you don't open the first six to check. You know every locker is one width wide, so you walk 7 widths from the door and you are there. An array is that corridor in memory.
mentalModel.click: Same-size boxes in an unbroken row, so the box you want is at start + index × size and you can go straight to it.

glossary.definition: The number of a box, counting from 0. The first box is index 0, so a list of 5 has indexes 0 to 4.
The value stored in one box.
Side by side with no gaps. An array's boxes are contiguous in memory.
Where a box lives in memory, as a number. Address = start + index × size of one box.
How many boxes the array was built with. It is fixed. The size is how many of them are in use.
Copying elements one slot over to open a gap (insert) or close one (delete). Every shifted element is one step of work.

mentalModel.definition: An array is a fixed number of same-size slots stored next to each other in memory and numbered from 0. Because the slots are contiguous, the address of slot i is base + i × size, so reading or writing any slot takes the same constant time, O(1). The cost of that speed is rigidity: the capacity is fixed, inserting or deleting in the middle shifts every element after it (O(n)), and finding a value you only know by content means scanning, also O(n) in the worst case.

useWhen: You read or change items by their position, again and again.
The data is a plain list that mostly stays the same length.
The problem says "given an array" and asks you to scan, count, compare or rearrange it.
You know, or can bound, how many items there will be.
notWhen: You keep inserting or deleting in the middle of a long list. Every change shifts everything after it, so look at linked lists.
You look things up by a key, like a name or an id, instead of a position. Hash maps find them without scanning.
You ask the same "sum from here to there" question over and over. Precompute running totals with prefix sums instead of re-adding.

quiz.problem: Store the temperature for each of the last 365 days, then read the temperature of day 200 many times.
quiz.explanation: The day number is a position, and you only read by position. An array jumps straight to day 200 in one step.

quiz.problem: Given thousands of customer names, answer "is Priya a customer?" quickly, many times over.
quiz.explanation: You search by content, not by position. Scanning an array checks every name each time, while a hash map goes to the right bucket directly.

quiz.problem: A long list gets thousands of inserts and deletes at its front, and you never read by position.
quiz.explanation: In an array every front insert shifts the whole list. A linked list only rewires a couple of links.

quiz.problem: A list of numbers never changes. You get 100,000 questions of the form "what is the sum from index l to r?"
quiz.explanation: Re-adding each range is slow. Store running totals once, then every range sum is one subtraction.

quiz.problem: Find where a number sits in a sorted list of a million numbers as fast as you can.
quiz.explanation: The list is already sorted, so each question can throw away half of what is left. That is about 20 looks, not a million.

notes: Insert shown here. Delete is the mirror image: slide the elements after index i one slot left, then clear the last slot.
Access is O(1): address = base + i × size, so every index costs one jump.
Insert and delete are O(n) in the worst case because up to n elements shift. At the very end nothing has to move, so they are O(1) there.
Search by value is O(n): in the worst case every slot is looked at. A sorted array can do better with binary search.
Insert and delete work in place, so they use O(1) extra space. The array itself takes O(n). A full array can't grow: you would copy everything into a bigger one.

examples.title: Remove Element
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums and a value val, remove every occurrence of val in place. Return k, the number of elements not equal to val. The first k slots of nums must hold them, in any order.
approach: Deleting each 3 with a shift would cost O(n) per delete. Instead, make one pass and keep a write position for the next slot to fill.
Walk through the array with read. Whenever nums[read] is not val, copy it into nums[write] and move write on.
Here 3 is skipped, 2 goes to slot 0, 2 goes to slot 1, and the last 3 is skipped.
write ends at 2. The first 2 slots hold [2, 2], and whatever sits after them doesn't matter.

examples.title: Move Zeroes
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums, move all 0s to the end while keeping the order of the other numbers. Do it in place.
approach: Keep a write position: the slot where the next non-zero number belongs.
Walk through with read. When nums[read] is not 0, swap it with nums[write] and move write on.
Each non-zero number lands in the next free front slot, so their order never changes. The zeroes are pushed behind them by the swaps.
One pass, no extra array: 1, 3 and 12 go to slots 0, 1 and 2, and the zeroes end up at the back.

examples.title: Rotate Array
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums, rotate it to the right by k steps, in place.
approach: Shifting everything by one, k times, costs O(n × k). Three reversals do the same job in O(n).
First reduce k to k % n, so that rotating by n or more doesn't repeat laps.
Reverse the whole array: [7,6,5,4,3,2,1]. Then reverse the first k numbers: [5,6,7,4,3,2,1].
Finally reverse the remaining n - k numbers: [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. Each number was swapped a constant number of times.

conceptQuiz.question: Why can the computer read nums[500] as fast as nums[0]?
options: It keeps the first 500 boxes in a faster kind of memory.
Computers count so quickly that 500 steps don't show.
The boxes are the same size and side by side, so the address is start + 500 × size.
It sorts the boxes before it reads.
conceptQuiz.explanation: No counting happens. One multiply and one add give the address, and that costs the same for any index.

conceptQuiz.question: An array starts at address 2000 and each box takes 8 bytes. Where does index 5 live?
conceptQuiz.explanation: Skip 5 boxes of 8 bytes: 2000 + 5 × 8 = 2040. The result is 2005 if you forget the box size, and 2048 if you skip one box too many.

conceptQuiz.question: You insert a number at index 0 of an array that holds 100 numbers and has room to spare. How many numbers move?
conceptQuiz.explanation: Index 0 is the front, so every one of the 100 numbers shifts one slot right to make a gap. That is why insert is O(n).

conceptQuiz.question: Why does insert shift from the last number backwards, not from the front?
options: Starting at the end is faster.
Copying from the front would overwrite numbers that haven't moved yet.
Arrays only allow writes near the end.
The last number is always the biggest.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Copying nums[i] into nums[i + 1] first would destroy the old nums[i + 1]. Moving the last number into the free slot keeps every number safe.

conceptQuiz.question: You search an unsorted array of n numbers for a value that isn't there. How many slots do you look at?
conceptQuiz.explanation: Nothing tells you where the value might be, so you can only rule slots out by checking them. Not found means all n were checked.

practice.title: Running Sum of 1d Array
practice.insight: Each new total is the previous total plus one more number, so a single left-to-right pass is enough.

practice.title: Contains Duplicate
practice.insight: Scanning for repeats for every number is slow. Remember what you have seen and ask whether the current number is in there.

practice.title: Merge Sorted Array
practice.insight: The free room is at the end of the array, so fill from the back, taking the bigger number each time. Nothing gets overwritten.

practice.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
practice.insight: Equal numbers sit side by side. Use a write position and only copy a number when it differs from the one before it.

practice.title: Find Pivot Index
practice.insight: At each index, the right sum is the total minus the left sum minus the current number. Keep the left sum as you go.

practice.title: Product of Array Except Self
practice.insight: The answer at i is everything to its left times everything to its right. Build the left products in one pass and fold in the right products in another.

practice.title: Maximum Subarray
practice.insight: At each number decide: extend the run you have, or start fresh here. A run with a negative total only drags the next number down.

practice.title: First Missing Positive
practice.insight: Use the array as its own lookup: a number v between 1 and n belongs at index v - 1, so swap each one home and look for the first slot that is wrong.

overview: Explain why an array reaches any index in constant time.
Trace how inserting in the middle shifts later elements right.
Trace how deleting from the middle shifts later elements left.
Choose an array when you read by position and the length barely changes.
Spot when a prefix sum or hash map beats scanning the array.
